extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in folklore, humor studies, and linguistic/anthropological approaches to humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researching, analyzing, and theorizing about jokes and humor in folklore/anthropology: emphasizes empirical, testable analysis of joke texts, cautious theory-adoption, and movement from contextual description to generalizable explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive generalizations from materials (avoid a priori theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution against applying a priori theory to jokes; promote generalizations that emerge from studies of the materials themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the empirical material and let patterns and generalizations emerge; avoid imposing theoretical frameworks wholesale without testing how well they explain the data. Anti-pattern: evangelizing a new theory from another field without checking its fit to the humor data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate incongruity as a core analytic concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to 'appropriate incongruities' as a broadly applicable structure of meaning that underlies humor (Oring's conceptualization of incongruity/incongruity-resolution theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate incongruity to identify what makes a text a joke (its ontology). Note antecedents in historical literature; treat it as a persuasive but not fully operationalized hypothesis to be tested against examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what a joke is versus what it does
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize theories that define the nature/identity of jokes (what a joke is) rather than only describing their social or psychological functions (what a joke does).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: incongruity theory addresses 'what humor is'; superiority or relief theories describe functions. Evaluations should check whether a theory explains the phenomenon's identity or only its effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed micro-analysis: take jokes apart
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly analyze jokes; 'take them apart' to see how they work rather than presenting isolated examples without dissection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide step-by-step analytic readings of joke texts to reveal incongruities, connections, and mechanics. Anti-pattern: giving an example joke but not analyzing its components and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyses must be convincing and testable
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic claims about jokes should be persuasive to readers and, where possible, formulated so they can be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analyses do not convince others, they fail as scholarship. Prefer formulations that permit empirical testing or comparison rather than purely speculative interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize core terms (e.g., 'appropriateness', 'incongruity')
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical terms need clearer operational definitions to be useful for testing and for tasks like computational recognition of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify measurable criteria for abstract terms; acknowledge when terms are underspecified. Oring notes inability to operationalize 'appropriate' and 'incongruity' is a problem for producing a full theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of simplistic computational operationalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution against computational approaches that operationalize incongruity as generic 'opposition' or simple binary linguistic oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that linguistic oppositions are ubiquitous and not all oppositions are salient for humor; computational models should target the specific kinds of salience/connection that produce humor, not crude plus/minus charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose and test hypotheses (revive hypothesis-driven work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage offering hypotheses about humor (not merely interpretations) and subjecting them to testing, continuing the mid-20th-century practice of hypothesis-driven folklore work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate hypotheses that can be evaluated against evidence and compare competing accounts. Historical precedent: 1960s–70s Journal of American Folklore essays that discussed hypotheses and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically evaluate theories borrowed from other disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically apply new theories from linguistics, literature, philosophy, etc.; assess how well external theories explain the humor material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test borrowed theoretical tools against the data; avoid evangelizing for outside theories without critical appraisal of fit, scope, and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on purely contextual/performance descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of approaches that remain microscopic, describing single performance encounters without producing broader, generalizable explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use performance-based fieldwork but aim to move beyond single-case description toward patterns and principles that apply across contexts. Anti-pattern: producing only decontextualized event descriptions that don't inform larger theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fieldwork to generate generalizable knowledge (don't fetishize fieldwork)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fieldwork/recording of performances is necessary but should be used to support larger explanatory claims rather than being an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate field-collected data into hypotheses and comparative claims. Beware of treating the mere fact of having done fieldwork as sufficient scholarly contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject interpretive readings to critical apparatus and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive approaches must be tested and validated: how do you know your interpretation is what people actually communicate when they tell a joke?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop methods for validating interpretations (e.g., audience reactions, speaker intent, comparative evidence). Avoid pure literary-style readings that lack ways of checking accuracy against communicative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt comparative and cross-cultural perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether joking phenomena are similar across cultures and whether findings are comparable beyond a single cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare materials from multiple cultures to assess generality of claims; do not assume insights from one cultural performance generalize without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask penetrating questions and pursue serious attempts at answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship should go beyond admiration of materials to pose hard questions and pursue substantive, rigorous answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move from descriptive enthusiasm about materials to analytical inquiry that seeks explanatory advances; evaluations should favor work that addresses deep questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise formats (e.g., essays) to focus argument and avoid padding
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay form can be productive: it forces a specific point, concision, and the ability to address multiple distinct questions across pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer focused pieces that illuminate a single question clearly rather than sprawling, padded texts. Benefit: allows multiple testable propositions across essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to aesthetic and cognitive qualities of jokes (beauty, brilliance, mental twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and analyze the aesthetic dimensions of jokes—their beauty, brilliance, and the cognitive movement that shifts listeners from X to Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appreciation and analysis of the cognitive twist and artistry in jokes as part of scholarly evaluation; this is both an object of study and a criterion for valuing material.
